1 Introduction
Few measurement models are as attractive and as distrusted as the bifactor model. Since
its rediscovery (Reise, 2012), it has been fit to ability batteries, psychopathology inventories,
and quality-of-life scales. It also wins the model comparisons it enters with remarkable
regularity: more than 90% of the time against the higher-order model in mental-abilities
batteries (Cucina & Byle, 2017). Yet the same literature documents chronic anomalies, with
a reported prevalence above 60% in applications (Eid et al., 2017). These include collapsed or
vanishing group factors, general factors that rotate into group factors, and loading patterns
that defy interpretation. Methodologists have raised three further concerns. The bifactor’s
fit advantage partly reflects its greater functional flexibility rather than structural truth
(Bonifay & Cai, 2017; Murray & Johnson, 2013). The higher-order model is the bifactor
plus a proportionality constraint (Gignac, 2016; Schmid & Leiman, 1957; Yung et al., 1999).
Standard information criteria can prefer the wrong member of the pair at realistic sample
sizes (Raykov et al., 2024).

Two literatures approach this problem from opposite identification philosophies, and both
descend from Schmid and Leiman (1957). The exploratory lineage identifies an unrestricted
loading matrix by rotation or constraint (Asparouhov & Muthén, 2026; Garcia-Garzon et

tion is post hoc. The partially exploratory lineage starts from the confirmatory pole: a few
anchors are estimated structure rather than rotation targets, the remaining pattern is se-
lected by regularization, and candidate structures grow from an anchored backbone through
a factor-structure sweep (Chen & Jin, 2026a). The positioning diference is what each de-
livers. Exploratory hierarchical approaches condition on a supplied count and ask which
representation is recoverable at that count. The present approach treats count uncertainty

sible adjacent counts, with no stable structure delivered as the explicit output when none
exists, and the bifactor decision conditional on the delivered structure (Table 1). Relative

the distinguishability theory, the stable-structure estimand with its persistence indicators
and explicit non-delivery output, the calibrated end-to-end evaluation, and the recast of the
bifactor decision as a necessity question.

Everything that follows rests on keeping four questions apart. Identifiability asks whether a
specified model’s parameters can be recovered; count selection asks which candidate counts
deserve examination; structural stability asks whether approximately the same configuration
persists across adjacent counts on the observed data; and distinguishability asks whether

5 Discussion
Selection is not delivery: the gain rule identifies a neighborhood worth examining, not by
itself a structure worth interpreting. Study 3 makes the inference quantitative: a unanimous
count coexists with a structure that fails to reproduce, in up to 31.0% of replications once
interference is added, and the empirical bfi behaves identically. Behind it sits the paper’s
through-line about the bifactor’s practical troubles: fit advantages that do not replicate,
anomalous solutions, and spurious general factors. These are not estimator pathologies to
be tuned away. They are surface expressions of a population-level property with a sharp
suficient condition and a partly characterized boundary. Distinguishability lives in the
within-cluster loading-ratio patterns. It dies at the reducible boundary that the higher-order
model occupies (Proposition 1), it survives whenever every cluster departs from proportion-
ality (Theorem 1), and mixed configurations require the finer pattern analysis developed in
the Appendix.
Study 3 adds a second hazard with the same signature as the first and a diferent cause. Study
2’s under-count result showed a missing first-order factor manufacturing a general factor;

can flow into the general column, whether its source is a merged cluster or a residual doublet.
